extracted.intended_audience: vehicle manufacturers, conformity testing laboratories, safety engineers, and other industry stakeholders involved in FMVSS No. 210 seat belt anchorage compliance testing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory decisions on (a) defining allowable placement zones for torso and pelvic body blocks at preload, (b) preload/test forces and timing, and (c) related test-setup, safety, and procedure requirements for FMVSS No. 210 anchorage strength testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference point for zone location (SgRP)
rubrics_metrics.description: The zones are specified in relation to the SgRP (seating reference point), a design point determined by the vehicle manufacturer that represents a specific landmark near the hip of a 50th percentile adult male seated in the driver's seat. NHTSA decided to use the SgRP and not the torso belt adjusted height (TBAH) or the H-point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and guidance: commenters noted TBAH variability across non-school-bus seats and concerns with H-point determination variability. NHTSA concluded SgRP provided a more adequate torso location and used it as the reference when developing the final zones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of zones to a range of vehicle and seat designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Zones must be feasible and practicable for a wide variety of motor vehicles and seat configurations (including passenger vehicles and, to the extent validated, some heavy vehicles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA's zones are based on body block data from a range of vehicles and were mathematically expanded to accommodate a wider range; validated on three heavy-vehicle seats. Although not tested on every medium/heavy truck type, the agency concluded the zones are valid for a wide range. Manufacturers are responsible for ensuring compliance at all points in the zones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting body block position at preload
rubrics_metrics.description: Body block placement at preload is affected by vehicle-specific parameters (seat design, seat cushion contour, bolster shape), seat belt system geometry and routing, seat belt payout/retractor extension, the mass/design of torso and pelvic blocks, and the hardware used to connect blocks to force actuators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical setup guidance: mark the belt at the D-ring and lock to desired length to control fore/aft position; choose replacement webbing/cable length to achieve required fore/aft position; routing of belt on torso block can be used for small adjustments; labs use positioning aids or manual positioning to achieve preload positions. NHTSA found torso block positioning not sensitive to block mass within the observed range; connection method (e.g., chains) did not have meaningful effect on preload position in agency testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of zones, variability of test results, and compliance responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The final zones are modest in size and specified (torso target point: 530 mm x 240 mm x 245 mm; pelvic target point: 340 mm x 205 mm x 145 mm). Any variability in pass/fail at different locations in the zone reflects vehicle performance; manufacturers must ensure compliance across the entire zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA ran indicant tests at longitudinal extremes and observed no effect on meeting load requirements. The refined procedure reduces permissible test conditions compared to unconstrained prior practice and therefore narrows variability of outcomes. Historical failure rates for anchorage testing are low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory safety and minimizing technician exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Positioning body blocks while preload is applied can create confined, complex setups that increase technician exposure; test procedures should consider laboratory safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use positioning aids, lasers, Faro Arm, or other methods to minimize technician involvement during preload application and positioning; these measures reduce safety risk and test setup effort rather than installation effort. Avoid adjusting blocks while high test forces are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory test procedure language and public process
rubrics_metrics.description: NHTSA will issue the final rule without an additional pre-final draft workshop; the research report docketed with the notice of availability contains the exact zone specifications and extensive information about test procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laboratory test procedure documents may include informal laboratory procedures, but for manufacturer certification the regulatory test procedure in the final rule controls. NHTSA is not required to publish proposed regulatory text under the APA in every instance and deemed additional public comment unnecessary here.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mutual contact at end of preload (avoid interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test procedure specifies that the body blocks must not be in contact at the end of the preload force application (i.e., before the higher test force is applied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency recognizes blocks may touch after the higher test loads (>1,335 N) begin and are being held; to prevent preload contact, adjust belt alignment on torso block or use a positioning aid. NHTSA will not generally prohibit contact after test loads start because of technician safety concerns when adjusting under full load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pushing body blocks against seatback / cinching belt method
rubrics_metrics.description: NHTSA declined to adopt the ECE R14-style method of pushing blocks into the seat back and cinching the belt tight as a mandatory setup step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: cinching blocks against integrated seat belts could affect seat structure and anchorage performance; such a method is vague and could reduce objectivity/enforceability compared to specifying positions under preload. NHTSA seeks clear, objective, enforceable positions when preload is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torso body block pivot point and block design flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory text does not mandate a specific torso block pivot point location, weight, or detailed design; laboratories may continue to use existing block styles (yoke-style rear pull or front-pull) and weights (observed 7.7 kg to 13.7 kg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA's testing found different pivot styles position slightly differently (~15 mm average) but the finalized zones account for this variation. Specifying a pivot point is declined to preserve lab flexibility and because zones already accommodate observed variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seat belt buckle interference and replacement webbing option
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures should allow avoiding seat belt buckle interference with body blocks when positioning in the zone; where buckle interference cannot be avoided, the seat belt assembly may be replaced with a material of equal or greater strength (e.g., steel cable) to transfer loads to anchorages for compliance testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA found zones permit block placement to avoid buckle interference in most cases; positioning devices, spacers, or manual manipulation were considered in zone development. Use replacement webbing/material when necessary to prevent buckle damage during required test loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preload magnitude, test force magnitudes, ramp-up, and hold time
rubrics_metrics.description: FMVSS No. 210 test forces remain: 22,241 N for Type 1 pelvic loading and 13,345 N on lap and shoulder for Type 2 belts; the force must be attained in not more than 30 seconds and maintained for 10 seconds. The final regulatory text specifies a preload force of 1,335 N for both pelvic and torso body blocks for testing Type 1 and Type 2 belts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA evaluated higher preloads (e.g., 2,224 N) and found little effect on block position, but 2,224 N could begin to deform some seats; therefore NHTSA decided not to increase preload and set the preload at 1,335 N. The laboratory practice of applying a preload equal to 10% of the required target load historically remains informative, but the final text fixes preload at 1,335 N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning devices and methods are optional; labs have flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: NHTSA considered but declined to require a standardized positioning device or mandating redesign of torso blocks; instead, test laboratories are given flexibility to use positioning aids, simple fixtures, hoists, or manual methods as appropriate to the vehicle environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency research showed simple fixtures can aid initial position but required preload positions could be achieved without them; choice of method may vary by vehicle and laboratory preference. IMMI's proposed mass reduction or standardized device not mandated.

rubrics_metrics.name: FEA-based manufacturer-specific positioning not required for labs
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite element analysis (FEA) modeling used by manufacturers to establish body block positions is not a viable requirement for NHTSA testing laboratories, and NHTSA will not require labs to replicate manufacturer-specific FEA-based positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring FEA would necessitate collecting detailed seat design information for every trim/package and increase burden and cost; NHTSA will use objective zone positions instead of manufacturer-specific FEA-derived placements.
